turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I guess I'm here because... for almost two years now, I’ve been completely unable to shake this certainty that a few people in my ensemble are quietly undermining my work. It all started right after the big commission. 

Which, by the way, was a massive undertaking. I had to write 40 minutes of original music for a chamber orchestra, and I basically lived on cold brew and bagels for three months. There's this little deli down the street from my apartment that makes the absolute best everything bagels, but they always run out by 10 AM, so you have to get there early. I tried making my own bagels once, actually. The boiling part is just a huge hassle, getting the malt syrup ratio right... 

But anyway, yeah, after that commission, they started doing things. Subtle things. Using schedule changes, messing with the seating choices, making these little comments in rehearsals just to sabotage me. And they try to cover their tracks, too. They’ll show me emails or notes that supposedly explain why a rehearsal was moved or why the cellist had to sit somewhere else, but I know what's really going on. 

It’s exhausting. Honestly, almost as exhausting as trying to find parking near our rehearsal space these days. The city put in all these new bike lanes, which I guess is great for cyclists, but it took away half the street parking, so now I have to circle the block for twenty minutes just to unload my scores.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, unshakeable belief that colleagues are sabotaging their work, even when presented with contradictory evidence like emails or notes.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, frequently drifting off-topic to discuss unrelated details like making bagels, malt syrup ratios, and city parking issues.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: When you think about these people undermining your work, do you ever have any doubt that this is actually happening, or are you completely certain it's real?
turns.patient_response:
Doubt? No, I... I don't have any doubt at all. I'm completely certain. Like I was saying, for almost two years now, I just haven't been able to shake this absolute certainty about it. Ever since that commission, they’ve been using those schedule changes, the seating choices, the little comments... it's all designed to quietly undermine my work. And yeah, they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it, like, 'Oh, the cellist had to move because of a draft,' but I know what's actually happening. 

Speaking of those emails, actually, our ensemble's email server is an absolute nightmare. We use this ancient domain host that constantly flags important messages as spam. I actually missed a grant application deadline last year because the notification went straight to my junk folder. I mean, who still uses a POP3 server these days? I tried telling the board we need to migrate to a cloud-based system, maybe just basic Google Workspace, but they act like I'm asking them to learn ancient Greek or something. It's exactly like when I tried to get them to upgrade our acoustic shells, which are practically falling apart... 

Wait, what were you asking? Oh, right, if I have doubts. No, no doubts. I know exactly what they're up to, even with their little fake paper trails.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses absolute certainty that others are undermining their work and maintains this belief even when presented with contradictory evidence (emails/notes explaining the situations).
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality by drifting from the topic of the emails as evidence into a long, unrelated tangent about the ensemble's email server, POP3, and acoustic shells before losing track of the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever actually heard these people saying things about you, or seen them doing things to sabotage your work directly—like with your own eyes or ears—or is it more that you piece together what they're doing from the schedule changes and other clues?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, I haven't like... caught them whispering about me on a hot mic or anything. They're way too careful for that. I just piece it together from all the clues, the seating arrangements, the schedules. 

Which is actually kind of ironic because the acoustics in our rehearsal hall are so bizarre, you'd think I'd overhear everything anyway. It's this old converted church, and if you stand near the back where the pews used to be, there's this weird parabolic effect where you can hear a pin drop all the way on the stage. I was reading this whole article last month about architectural acoustics in 19th-century buildings, and they apparently used to mix horsehair into the plaster to dampen the reverberation. Horsehair! Can you imagine being the guy whose job it was to source and mix that? 

I'm actually terribly allergic to horses, by the way. I went to a petting zoo for a friend's birthday when I was seven, and my eyes swelled completely shut. My mom had to practically carry me to the car, and we ended up at this walk-in clinic on a Sunday afternoon. Sunday clinics are just the absolute worst, aren't they? The waiting room always smells like stale bleach and those ancient magazines that have been handled by a thousand sick people. I think I had to take that cherry-flavored liquid Benadryl for a week, and I still can't stand the taste of artificial cherry because of it. It totally ruined cherry soda for me.

But anyway... no, I don't need to hear them say it out loud or catch them red-handed. The proof is right there in how they keep shifting things around. You just have to know how to read between the lines.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient maintains a fixed belief of being sabotaged, piecing it together from 'clues' and 'reading between the lines' rather than direct evidence.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing or seeing the people directly saying or doing things against them.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality, wandering off-topic from rehearsal hall acoustics to horsehair, allergies, walk-in clinics, and cherry soda before returning to the question.

turns.doctor_question: When you think about all the ways these people are undermining your work, do the different things they're doing—the schedule changes, the seating, the comments—do they all fit together into one clear plan they have against you, or do they seem more like separate, unrelated incidents?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I'm not really sure if it's one big, coordinated master plan, or if they just... take the opportunities to mess with things as they come. I haven't really thought about it like some giant conspiracy board with red string connecting everything, you know? 

Speaking of string, I was actually trying to organize my studio cables last weekend, because I have this massive bin of XLR and MIDI cables that just turn into a complete rat's nest the second you look away. It's like that thing where headphones tangle themselves in your pocket, but multiplied by a hundred. I ended up ordering these little velcro cable ties online, but the company sent me the completely wrong color. I specifically chose matte black so they'd blend in on stage, and they sent me this obnoxious neon green. It looks absolutely ridiculous. It actually looks exactly like the carpets at this laser tag place I used to go to in middle school. 

We went there for my twelfth birthday, I think, and I was running backward away from my brother and completely tripped over this blacklight fixture. Sprained my ankle so badly I had to wear one of those giant orthopedic boots for six weeks. And it was right in the middle of marching band season! I was playing snare drum back then, and trying to march in a heavy boot while carrying a drum harness is just... well, it's terrible for your posture, for one thing. I had to go to a chiropractor for like a year after that, and he had this weird obsession with essential oils. The whole office smelled intensely like eucalyptus and peppermint. 

But... wait, sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, their plan. Yeah, I don't know if they actually sat down and mapped it all out together in a room. I just know what they're doing when I see the schedules and the seating changes.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient maintains their fixed belief that others are intentionally undermining them through schedule and seating changes, even if they aren't sure it's a coordinated master plan.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits marked derailment and tangentiality, drifting from the phrase 'red string' to studio cables, a laser tag place, a childhood injury, and a chiropractor before losing their train of thought entirely.

turns.doctor_question: If I were to tell you that I spoke with some of these ensemble members and they said they weren't actually trying to undermine you—that the schedule changes were just logistical and the seating was random—how would you respond to that? Would it change what you believe is happening, or would you still be certain they're undermining you?
turns.patient_response:
I'd tell you that they're lying. I mean, of course they'd say that to you. They're not just going to admit it. Even if they show you those same emails or notes they show me, the ones that supposedly explain why they had to move the cellist or change the rehearsal time... I wouldn't believe it, and it wouldn't change my mind. Like I said, I'm here because for almost two years now, I just haven't been able to shake this absolute certainty about it. Ever since that commission, they've been using those schedule changes and seating choices and those little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work. 

It's actually kind of like how people lie on their resumes, you know? Like, everyone pads their skills a little bit. I remember when I was hiring a copyist for a piece a few years ago, this one guy claimed he was an expert in Sibelius software. But when he sent back the first movement, the formatting was an absolute disaster. The staves were colliding, the dynamics were completely misaligned... it looked like a child had just dragged and dropped symbols randomly. 

I actually ended up having to redo the whole thing myself in Dorico, which is honestly a vastly superior program anyway once you get past the learning curve. The way it handles condensing scores is just brilliant. Although, the subscription model for software these days is really getting out of hand. It feels like you don't actually own anything anymore, you're just renting the right to use it. I was looking at my bank statement last month, and I have like fourteen different subscriptions going. Netflix, Spotify, the New York Times, this weird artisanal coffee delivery service my sister got me for Christmas... 

She always gets me the most random gifts. One year she bought me this indoor hydroponic herb garden because I mentioned I liked fresh basil in my pasta. It had this incredibly bright LED grow light that was on a timer, and it would turn on at exactly 4:00 AM every morning. It was so bright it would literally wake me up, like an alien abduction was happening in my kitchen. I eventually had to give it to my neighbor because I wasn't getting any sleep. 

But yeah... no, I wouldn't believe them. I know what they're doing, no matter what kind of innocent explanation they try to give you.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly states they would not believe contradictory evidence and maintain an 'absolute certainty' that they are being undermined, demonstrating a fixed belief.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangentiality, drifting from the topic of being undermined to resumes, music software, subscriptions, and a hydroponic herb garden before finally returning to the original point.
